body.heading: Charge builds in the cloud
paragraphs: Inside a thundercloud, rising and falling air tosses ice crystals and soft hail past each other in furious turbulence. Their collisions strip and transfer electric charge, gradually separating the cloud into a mostly negative base and a positive top — like a battery the size of a mountain.

Air is normally an excellent insulator, which is why the charge can build so high. But when the electric field grows strong enough, the air itself breaks down into a conductive path, and the stored energy escapes all at once.

body.heading: A bolt in steps
paragraphs: A faint leader reaches down from the cloud in quick steps, ionising a channel. When it nears the ground, a streamer rises to meet it — and the main return stroke surges up that channel at a sizeable fraction of the speed of light. That brilliant surge is the flash you see, and it heats the air to roughly five times the surface temperature of the Sun.

Most flashes never touch the ground at all; they jump within or between clouds. The ones that do are why the safety rule is absolute: when thunder roars, get indoors, because the spark can strike kilometres ahead of the rain.

takeaway: Lightning is a sudden discharge of electric charge built up inside storm clouds, flashing through a channel of ionised air.
